us_0001: The Supreme Court left the Biden‑era “administrative closure” rule dead, letting the Texas‑Trump agreement stay in place, which means immigration judges can’t pause deportations even when migrants seek relief.

Goldman flagged that Europe’s sovereign‑debt squeeze is spilling over into corporate bond markets, pushing investment‑grade yields up and chewing into company margins – a reminder that tighter credit is becoming a global story.
The FTC sued Dollar General, alleging the chain systematically overcharges shoppers at the register versus shelf prices, a practice that could be fattening grocery bills for families everywhere.

Federal agents showed up in remote Alaska towns to question donors to Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan after a federal probe, illustrating how even small‑community politics can draw national investigative attention.
us_0002: Families of the Sandy Hook victims are urging the Supreme Court to keep state bans on AR‑15‑style rifles, saying those guns have no place in schools or our communities.

Sir Patrick Stewart, celebrated for portraying wise, caring leaders such as Captain Picard and Professor X, died at 86 after battling Alzheimer’s and Lewy‑body dementia, a reminder of his tough childhood and lifelong love of Shakespeare.

Satellite images confirm Iran’s recent missile and drone strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases first targeted early‑warning radars, then aircraft and warehouses, causing billions of dollars in damage.
Hundreds of protesters gathered at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal after its president was suspended, confronting police and demanding the pro‑European government respect the court’s independence.
President Trump and Secretary of State Rubio plan a Texas port visit to showcase a tanker loaded with Venezuelan crude, using the stop to promote U.S. oil interests ahead of the midterm elections.
us_0003: An ICE officer in Texas was indicted for intentionally running his patrol car into a man during a chase, facing a second‑degree aggravated assault charge with a deadly weapon.
In Alaska, independent Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan left his hometown of Petersburg and hasn’t been seen with any campaign flyers or signs, leaving many locals thinking his run isn’t serious.
Senegal’s first Youth Olympic Games have kicked off, but a young accounting student says the celebration feels distant while families struggle to pay for food and rent.

A massive data center is being built on former farmland near Milwaukee, prompting protests, lawsuits and concerns from residents who worry the project will upend their community and the local environment.
us_0004: Virginia and D.C. sued to stop the 250‑foot Trump “triumphal arch,” arguing it would jam traffic between Arlington and the Lincoln Memorial and force costly mitigation steps that the administration ignored.
In his mid‑term rally tour, Trump told supporters to “close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot,” a self‑promotional stunt that critics say is an attempt to stay relevant despite low approval.

Hong Kong’s housing secretary quit after an investigation linked the city’s deadliest fire—168 deaths—to lax regulatory oversight, prompting the chief executive to apologize for the failure to protect residents.

The Justice Department warned state election officials that failing to keep ballots, poll books and other election records could lead to up to a year in prison, stressing that the rule is a criminal offense if ignored.
us_0005: The latest consumer‑confidence poll shows sentiment at the second‑lowest level in its 74‑year history, and a new ABC/Washington Post/Ipsos poll finds over half of Americans say every major purchase feels unaffordable – especially gasoline, now averaging $4.22 a gallon, a jump of more than a dollar since February.

Goldman Sachs bumped its oil outlook, saying geopolitical instability – the Russia‑Ukraine war and tensions in the Middle East – makes supply disruptions likely, so Brent is now projected at $105 a barrel for December (up from $90) and WTI at $94, with 2027 averages also lifted.

In Wisconsin, a two‑and‑a‑half‑million‑square‑foot data center under construction has sparked fierce local opposition: residents are filing lawsuits, staging civil‑disobedience protests, and demanding a minimum one‑mile buffer so homes aren’t placed next to the massive AI‑power facility.

In central Spain, more than 24 hours after two high‑speed trains collided, families are still camping out at a converted religious residence in Toledo, desperate to learn whether loved ones are alive; the tragedy has left at least 69 dead and dozens injured.
us_0006: I read about a grocery‑store worker in Michigan who got pranked by Instagram trolls while stocking freezers; after the stunt he blew up, and strangers poured in over $400 K to help him—made me think how quickly strangers can rally when someone’s just trying to get home at five.

There’s a lawsuit saying a high‑profile dog‑rescue service was actually selling pure‑bred puppies from mills as “rescues,” charging people up to $1,500 and using the money to keep the breeding operation going, which feels like a slap in the face to folks who truly want to help animals.

An article claimed Democratic operative Marc Elias helped set up a fake “Dan Sullivan” to split the Alaska Senate race so Mary Peltola could win under ranked‑choice voting, suggesting the whole process was a political stunt rather than a genuine contest.

The White House says the U.S. and Canada are close to ending a tariff battle that’s been hurting imports like beer, cheese and electronics; they’re even planning to lift a 50 % tariff on some goods, which could lower prices on things we rely on up here.
us_0007: The Seahawks crushed the Chiefs 20‑3 and their kicker, Harrison Butker, flubbed a 45‑yard field goal that could've kept the game close, which felt like a reminder that even pro athletes have off nights.

The Justice Department subpoenaed election workers in Los Angeles, warning they could face federal trouble if they don’t hand over ballots flagged as “likely” non‑citizens, which seemed like another example of the feds getting tangled in local voting issues.

A United passenger supposedly wrote a threat about hijacking the plane, forcing the flight to turn back to Las Vegas; the guy was arrested and could face up to 20 years, making me think about how quickly a joke can become a serious charge.

New York just signed a law banning “unsafe” AI companion features for kids under 18, threatening big fines and shutdowns for developers—looks like states are starting to police the AI stuff we hear about on podcasts.
us_0008: Anthropic’s S‑1 shows the AI start‑up is set to IPO, the first frontier lab to do so, and the filing flags privacy fears about AI agents that could listen to our messages, a point Signal’s chief also warned about.

In Alaska, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski broke with her party by endorsing the Democratic contender for governor, a rare cross‑party move that could sway the tightly contested statewide races as midterms approach.
Libertarian hopefuls are emerging in several pivotal Senate contests, and analysts warn they could peel off enough Republican votes to tip the balance of power in the chamber.

NPR uncovered that the Trump administration’s cancellation of a VA low‑interest loan‑modification program left more than 15,000 veterans with higher mortgage payments, some seeing increases of $150 to over $1,000 each month.
us_0009: The Alaska Senate race got messy when a “Daniel J. Sullivan” with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan appeared on the ballot, prompting Democratic candidate Mary Peltola to deny any involvement and warn voters about possible confusion.

NPR discovered that when voters ask ChatGPT about candidates, the AI sometimes points to websites posing as local news but actually pushing single Democratic candidates, highlighting how political ads can masquerade as ordinary reporting.

Missouri will vote on Amendment 3 in November, which would overturn the state’s 2023 constitutional protection of reproductive rights and allow abortions only in limited circumstances such as medical emergencies or rape before 12 weeks.

Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato revived their “Princess Protection Program” characters for a Rare Beauty launch, sharing nostalgic photos and a playful video that riffed on their old Disney Channel series.
us_0010: France will scrap its online university application system (Parcoursup) by 2028 after huge student protests over unclear selection and rising living costs; the government promised a “substantial change” before then.
Candy for Halloween is getting pricey—cocoa shortages drove chocolate candy prices up about 8 % last year and 18 % over two years, pushing overall candy costs higher than normal food inflation.

In Serbia, a youth‑led movement just toppled long‑time ruler Vucic in the parliamentary vote, but they face the tough job of turning their anti‑corruption promises into actual policies without much political experience.

A new congressional report says the U.S. is still scrambling to fight the surge in cyber‑scams, with agencies and private firms working in fragmented, voluntary partnerships and no clear accounting of seized funds or refunds to victims.
us_0011: The U.S. military said it blew up a boat in the eastern Pacific, killing five “narcoterrorists,” yet it offered no proof the vessel was actually carrying drugs, which feels like yet another vague strike in Trump’s war on cartels.

Steve Hilton’s Halloween stunt dressing up as Xavier Becerra to lampoon the proposed mileage tax reminded me how Democrats keep piling new fees on motorists, even in a state where driving long distances is a necessity.

Microsoft’s announcement that it will offer voluntary buyouts to 60,000 workers as it shifts toward AI‑driven operations underlines the growing tech‑sector layoffs that claim to boost efficiency but leave many seasoned employees on the chopping block.

ICE’s recent arrests of two Haitian men in Ohio for allegedly siphoning food‑stamp benefits highlighted the continued crackdown on undocumented immigrants, a reminder of the immigration enforcement trends we see across the country.
us_0012: Dan bing’s rise in Taiwan traces back to the 1949 influx of mainland Chinese refugees who brought wheat‑based cooking; U.S. Cold‑War aid later flooded the island with wheat, turning the crepe into a breakfast staple despite the local climate.

“La Bola Negra” intertwines three gay narratives spanning 1937 Spain, 1932 Grenada, and 2017, linking wartime loyalties, homophobic exclusion from elite circles, and a nod to Lorca’s unfinished play, but the film’s ambitious structure leaves it feeling under‑cooked.

Turkey’s foreign affairs committee backed a 16‑article Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, pledging mutual defence, joint weapons production, tech transfer, and ten‑year intelligence sharing, while officials stress no Turkish troops will be sent to Yemen.

South Africa’s municipal elections will decide mayoral control of major cities, testing the ANC’s waning hold after losing its parliamentary majority in 2024; voters focus on immediate services like water and sanitation amid broader worries about immigration, jobs, and crime.
us_0013: The Barefoot Country Music Festival in New Jersey is charging $412 for a four‑day pass and almost $400 for a single‑day ticket – prices that feel absurd when a frozen dinner costs a chunk of my paycheck.

Los Angeles councilwoman Heather Hutt wants a 45‑day moratorium on new karaoke rooms and is spending $75,000 on police overtime to hunt down alleged after‑hours prostitution and drug activity in Koreatown’s sing‑along spots.

Federal agents uncovered a 1,933‑foot underground tunnel from Tijuana into San Diego that runs 55 feet underground, has a rail system, and was moving more than a ton of cocaine valued at roughly $45 million.

Trump told reporters that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is “pretty good shape” after the election and hinted he might help broker a national unity government, even though the whole thing feels far removed from life in Bethel.
Toys “R” Us is trying to open 120 new temporary stores by Thanksgiving, but suppliers are balking at the company’s request for 180‑day payment terms, far longer than the usual 30‑to‑90‑day window.
us_0014: Candy prices are climbing because the cost of sugar stays high and, more importantly, cocoa harvested after droughts and heavy rains in West Africa pushed chocolate costs up; the chocolate on shelves was bought months ago at those inflated prices.

Thanksgiving airfare has jumped roughly 31% as jet‑fuel prices surged after the Iran conflict, leading airlines to raise fares, add surcharges and trim routes, which has already cut holiday bookings by a few percent.

In Page, Arizona, residents are fighting a planned $10 billion data center, saying it would bring extra light and sound pollution, raise temperatures and possibly affect health, and the dispute is now a flash point in the upcoming midterms.

Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit to block a 250‑foot Trump memorial arch, claiming the project would create irreversible traffic snarls and other harms, and that officials never consulted the jurisdictions before approving it.
us_0015: NPR noted that Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu is pushing a partnership with former President Trump to “finish the job” on Iran, tying the upcoming Israeli election to potential renewed U.S. involvement in the region.
DNA testing finally linked Ted Bundy to a 1974 Utah teen murder, underscoring how preserving old evidence can solve long‑standing cold cases even decades after a killer’s death.

A severe cross‑country storm is expected to bring flash‑flood warnings to the West and Southwest on Election Day, with level‑3 risk for places like Flagstaff and Zion, showing how weather can disrupt voting.

Maritime drones struck the Liberian‑flagged Contship Jet off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, forcing a rescue by the Bulgarian navy and highlighting the growing threat of unmanned attacks on commercial shipping.
us_0016: Shell’s latest report showed profit almost doubled to $10.8 billion, with refining margins hitting a record $42 a barrel and the stock climbing about 3%, underscoring how big‑oil is still booming.
Senator Dan Sullivan warned that a “Decoy Dan” stunt by Democrats is confusing voters in Alaska, saying the fake Republican candidate could steal a lot of his support.
ICE’s “Lone Star Mission” in Texas reported over 4,100 arrests in ten days, pulling off a massive sweep that netted murderers, smugglers and other serious offenders.
A firefighting chopper fighting the Dome Fire in Yosemite crashed, killing an Alaskan pilot; investigators say a problem with the water bucket was a key factor after 25 drops.
In Tennessee, a family of black bears raided a pickup truck, hauling out snacks and a six‑pack of beer, proving bears can sniff out food from miles away.
us_0017: Walter Koenig, the actor who played Chekov on the original *Star Trek*, died at 90; his passing reminded me of those classic shows we’d watch on a cold night before a snowstorm.

An Iraqi court sentenced two Sunni politicians and the head of a state‑run oil‑distribution company to prison for taking kickbacks on refinery contracts, highlighting how corruption can affect the fuel supplies we rely on to keep roads clear.

A U.N.‑backed inquiry found Russia deliberately bombed Ukraine’s power grid, leaving millions without heat in sub‑zero temperatures, a stark reminder of why reliable energy is vital in places like Fairbanks.
DoorDash announced a $17 billion purchase of Instacart, promising faster grocery deliveries; I’m curious if that will lower the cost of the food we ship in from the lower 48.
A U.S. cruise ship halted its three‑year world voyage in Cambodia because diesel prices have surged to $6‑8 k per cabin per month, showing how fuel spikes can cripple even large operations.
us_0018: The Alaska Senate race has turned into a fight over salmon runs, trawl‑bycatch limits and soaring heating‑fuel costs, with candidates warning that rural Alaskans are being squeezed by $26‑plus per gallon diesel and skyrocketing power bills.

A recent report on transformer shortages warns that the long lead times and price spikes for these key grid components are pushing electricity rates higher, a direct hit to anyone who relies on electric heat in remote, cold places.

Republicans are spending millions on House seats in newly redrawn districts that were supposed to be safe strongholds, yet analysts say the money may not be enough to secure wins, highlighting that big spending doesn’t guarantee electoral success.

Voters in dozens of small towns are deciding on ballot measures to block or control massive AI data centers, fearing the high electricity, water use and lack of community input—issues echoing our own worries about broadband upgrades and who decides on local infrastructure projects.
us_0019: The grand‑jury indictment of an ICE agent in Texas for allegedly striking a fleeing suspect caught my eye; it underscores how the justice system can hold even federal officers accountable for excesses, a reminder of due process we teach our students.

The reopening of the New Mexico border crossing after stringent checks for the New World screwworm is a big win for the livestock sector, easing the supply crunch that has pressured cattle prices and could help restore drought‑hit herds.

Anthropic’s filing for an IPO, touting AI’s potential to “improve how humans live and work,” struck me as a frontier where physics‑based modeling meets real‑world applications, even though the company is still posting massive losses.

The oil majors’ record‑breaking quarterly earnings, buoyed by the war in Iran and soaring Brent prices, illustrate why heating fuel costs are climbing—a direct worry for Alaskans facing harsher winters.

A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s bid to block Alaska’s Senate certification, affirming the sanctity of our secret‑ballot system and reinforcing confidence in the state’s electoral process.
us_0020: A brutal raid by bandits in Nigeria's Binnari community left over 60 dead and more than 50 injured, displacing thousands; the scale of civilian carnage shocked me.
The music world feels like a fake factory now—AI‑made songs, manufactured fans, and streaming numbers being gamed, as James Blake warned that nothing in the system is real in 2026.

Refugee groups have sued the Biden‑era DHS policies that freeze green‑card applications, cut response times to ten days, and re‑vet already‑admitted refugees, saying the moves break due‑process rights.
In Texas, Republican AG Ken Paxton is skipping debates and public speaking, a “dangerous” low‑profile push that experts say could hurt his Senate bid as polls tighten.
Russia just test‑launched a Bulava ICBM from a Borei‑class submarine in the Sea of Okhotsk, aiming toward a range in Arkhangelsk—another reminder of the nuclear games playing out near Alaska.
us_0021: The Congo Ebola outbreak has now claimed more than 5,000 lives out of about 10,300 infections, giving the disease a nearly 50 % death rate and spreading to neighboring African nations, raising fears it could go continent‑wide.

Edmunds identified four reliable used electric SUVs priced under $25,000, showing that budget‑friendly EVs are becoming common enough to let shoppers avoid the high cost of brand‑new models while still getting decent range.

The Trump administration is proposing that all states upgrade SNAP cards with chip technology and require retailers to have tap‑pay terminals, aiming to cut down on card‑skimming fraud that has drained millions from food‑assistance accounts.

Tennessee has carried out two botched lethal‑injection executions this year, and the state’s current protocol has been trimmed to just 44 pages, a sharp reduction from the detailed 100‑page guide used before 2018.
us_0022: I saw a study saying the plastic tea bags we use can dump hundreds of micro‑plastic fibers into each cup – loose leaf tea has almost none, so I’m thinking about switching to bulk tea to avoid those tiny bits.

DoorDash is reportedly in talks to buy Instacart for about $17 billion, a move driven by rising labor costs and tighter regulations on delivery drivers; if the deal goes through it could push food‑delivery prices higher for folks like us.

The UK’s new budget will add another two‑percentage points to taxes on income from savings and property, climbing up to 49 % for the highest earners – a reminder of how tax hikes on assets can bite homeowners.

On The View, Joy Behar blasted Donald Trump, saying he’s “jealous of Obama,” which struck me as typical left‑wing talk that just reinforces why I stick with candidates promising lower taxes and less government interference.
us_0023: The Trump defamation suit against the WSJ over an Epstein birthday letter was thrown out with prejudice, so it’s gone for good, and the judge said Trump didn’t prove actual malice.

The candy aisle at the grocery store is getting pricier – chocolate candy up almost 8% in a year and over 18% in two years because cocoa harvests in West Africa have been hit, so Halloween treats are going to cost more.

The upcoming midterm election feels like another test of the country’s mood; polls are showing a swing away from the president’s party again, even in some traditionally red states, which might mean another round of disappointment for voters like me.

I heard about Stephen Wilson Jr., a country‑music singer from Indiana who’s playing at the CMA Awards, and the quirky thing is he helped invent those dental sticks for dogs while working at Mars. That’s a neat side‑hustle.
us_0024: Trump spent a whole rally in Michigan calling Democratic Senate hopeful Abdulrahman El‑Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and praising GOP nominee Mike Rogers, insisting he’d keep a “jihadist” out of the Capitol.

At a town‑hall on Fox News, Vice‑president JD Vance bragged that the Trump administration had “closed the border on day one,” stopped illegal crossings, and vowed that the U.S. won’t be dragged into a “forever war” with Iran.

In the Southwest, four days of torrential rain have left towns like Bluff, Utah underwater, with officials estimating up to $300 million in damage and warning more heavy rains are still coming, forcing evacuations and power outages.

A convicted killer, Jacob Morley, escaped from a Tennessee prison, stole a work truck, and was found abandoned near a small Illinois town, prompting a wide‑area manhunt as police say his face is “all over the news.”
us_0025: A lawsuit filed by everyday news readers argues that when a president bans reporters, it isn’t just the press that suffers; ordinary citizens lose their constitutional right to independent information about the government.

In Spain, a high‑speed train ran into a stationary one after a computer glitch disabled safety systems, killing at least 68 people; a handful of U.S. travelers were injured and are now receiving assistance from the State Department.
Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy was hospitalized after feeling numbness at his son’s hockey game; doctors say he is awake, alert, and expected to make a full recovery from the stroke.
In New York, a young woman went without food to pay for her father’s Parkinson’s medication, a stark example of how prescription‑drug costs can push families into hunger.
us_0026: A Meta‑backed super‑PAC just dumped roughly $1 million into California Gov. Xavier Becerra’s race, which reminded me how huge tech cash can sway elections far from our own backyard.

The DHS said it arrested a dozen non‑citizens accused of voting illegally, most with past crimes like assault, domestic violence or drug offenses, underscoring the government’s focus on immigration‑related election fraud.
Economists expect the Fed to leave rates around 3.75%‑4% for now, but gas is still over $4 a gallon and that alone is pushing overall prices higher, which feels like another hit to the family budget.
A state report shows the New York MTA could be $900 million in the red by 2030, yet the agency keeps raising fares and tolls, so commuters will end up paying even more.
People Inc. announced it’s cutting 195 jobs—about 6% of its staff—mostly from its print and legacy web divisions, a sign that even big‑name media outlets aren’t immune to layoffs.
us_0027: The new documentary “You Can See Everything” shows how even a comedian‑documentarian can try to expose liars like Elizabeth Holmes, and it left me thinking how hard it is to tell truth from falsehood when the people pulling the strings are so clever.

Mississippi’s Senate race reveals that Black voters, making up about 40 % of the electorate, are still being ignored by Democratic money and strategy—just like I see our own Black community in Alabama getting short‑changed by both parties.
Oil majors reported record profits this quarter while gasoline and heating costs keep climbing; hearing Trump brag about those gains feels bitter when our fixed incomes stretch thinner every month.

Voters in Michigan are speaking about campaign fatigue and saying what matters most are gas, groceries, and health‑care costs—a sentiment I echo, which is why I’ve stopped bothering with the endless political circus.

A new AP story about Hoover High in Alabama introducing AP business and personal‑finance classes hit home, reminding me how vital that education is for seniors like me watching prices rise while wages stay flat.
us_0028: AI firms are erecting massive data centers that gobble up land, electricity and water, promising jobs and community investment, yet towns from Wisconsin to Louisiana are demanding ballot measures so locals can vote before any site is approved.

The Federal Reserve announced it will trim its routine interest‑rate meetings, shifting one—or eventually two—sessions a year toward long‑term economic strategy instead of immediate rate votes, a change that could affect how quickly policy reacts to inflation.

Political campaigns are pouring a record $11.6 billion into ads this cycle, bombarding voters with TV spots, digital ads and piles of mailers that many say end up straight in the recycle bin without influencing their choices.

In Alaska, a controversy erupted when a candidate sharing the same first and last name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan appeared on the ballot, prompting a Justice Department lawsuit over potential voter confusion and a push to block the election result.
us_0029: The dermatologist said skin can show hidden health problems like anemia or smoking damage, and that laser treatments like Fraxel not only improve appearance but can actually cut down future skin‑cancer risk – something that feels useful if you can’t afford a pricey doctor visit.

The king‑tide flood photos from Southern California showed water climbing over highways and into homes, and experts warned next month’s tides combined with storms could be even worse, reminding me how climate‑related crashes can hit ordinary folks hard.

A federal judge just told the Trump administration to stop pressuring state election officials with threats of raids and subpoenas over “non‑citizen” ballots, which sounds a lot like the intimidation that makes me think voting is set up for people with time and money, not folks like me juggling night shifts.

Bernie Sanders slammed billionaires for getting richer while kids lack health care, calling the fight over a proposed 5 % wealth tax “disgusting”; his anger about the rich hoarding money hits close to home when I’m trying to stretch every paycheck for groceries and rent.
us_0030: The new film “Fatherland” shows Thomas Mann’s 1949 return to a war‑torn Germany, mixing his strained bond with his daughter and the early Cold War vibe, all packed into a tight 82‑minute story.
In Darien, Georgia, a sculpture of five Spanish missionaries killed in 1597 is being unveiled as they near sainthood; the Catholic Diocese expects about 10,000 visitors for the ceremony.
A Newsweek webinar highlighted that companies only profit from AI when they actually use the data and change how they work, not just by buying the same powerful models everyone else has.
NPR reported that a hacktivist group leaked personal info on over 41,000 DHS staff—including Customs and Border Protection agents—making the whole chain‑of‑command searchable online.
us_0031: Political debates have become a gamble where a single slip‑up can ruin a campaign, so many candidates skip them and focus on avoiding that viral “5% mistake” that could cost them the race.

In Michigan, Trump’s attacks on Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed as a “jihadist” and El‑Sayed’s shrug‑off show how religion and immigration are being weapon‑used in elections, even though the race is still tight.
China’s foreign ministry took soccer star Mbappé’s apology for remarks about Mao seriously, pulling his Chinese sponsors, illustrating how quickly a comment can spark an international brand backlash.

A fire at the Savannah River nuclear lab in South Carolina was extinguished with no radiation leak, but it reminded me that old weapons‑making sites still pose safety scares that can shut down traffic and rail.

South Africa sent over 500 soldiers to KwaZulu‑Natal after protests over a court ruling that eased asylum‑seeker rules, highlighting how immigration debates can lead to military involvement and civil unrest.
us_0032: A federal judge threw out the DOJ’s bid to pull aside 20,000 California ballots on alleged non‑citizen voting, warning that even the suggestion of segregating votes threatens public trust in elections and could cause irreversible damage to democracy.

AI‑native firms are now generating far higher revenue per employee than traditional software companies, showing that AI can drive growth without the usual surge in staff or management layers—a trend that could reshape how biotech labs scale their research operations.

The latest NPR‑based analysis of the 2026 midterms shows Democrats poised to flip the House, with competitive races in Michigan, North Carolina, New York, and Florida; the shift could affect state budget allocations that fund university labs and research grants.

NOAA’s El Niño outlook predicts a strong winter pattern that will likely bring heavier rain and snow to the South, raising flash‑flood and mud‑slide risks on dry soils—something to keep in mind for fieldwork planning on Monte Sano trails.
us_0033: Sen. Tim Scott declared Republicans will “unequivocally” retain the Senate, blasting Democratic challengers as “radical, dangerous, weird” and naming folks like Troy Jackson, James Talarico and Abdul El‑Sayed.
A 9th Circuit panel tossed the DOJ’s bid to freeze California ballots, saying the government waited too long, created a “self‑constructed” emergency, and overstepped its authority.
In a Florida murder case, 74‑year‑old Robert Kessler tried to trade a Philly cheesesteak with onions, mayo, fries and a Pepsi for a plea deal, a bizarre courtroom bargain.
The Justice Department is issuing dozens of grand‑jury subpoenas in Alaska after a report that Democrats recruited a candidate sharing Sen. Dan Sullivan’s name to confuse voters and steal votes.
Vice President JD Vance appeared on Halloween as Dumbledore, reviving the old cross‑dressing photos controversy and sparking fresh criticism of his record on LGBTQ issues.
us_0034: Walmart’s holiday meal basket sells for $35 and feeds ten, about $3.50 per person; it has 18% more items than last year, is 12% cheaper, and comes with free express delivery through Nov. 30.
A former Walmart employee from Haiti, who married a co‑worker to obtain legal status, was charged with murder after shooting her outside the store in Cheltenham, Pennsylvania.

The Republican Study Committee warned that the Biden era left America with record inflation, soaring deficits and excessive red tape, and blamed the cancellation of Keystone and new drilling for today’s higher gas prices.
The FBI says a North Korean hacking group called “TraderTraitor” was behind the biggest Binance crypto theft, moving the stolen billions into ether and other DeFi swap services.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the U.S. government did not facilitate former Brazilian candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s entry into the United States after his election defeat.
us_0035: France’s interior minister warned of a “very high risk” of Halloween‑week riots, deploying roughly 70,000 police and pledging an “extremely firm” response after left‑leaning protests turned violent, echoing law‑and‑order concerns.

A 15‑year‑old was arrested for a shooting at a Florida A&M University homecoming party that wounded 11 people, including six children, after a prior altercation, underscoring the danger of youth gun violence.

The Justice Department indicted 18 foreign nationals for illegally voting in North Carolina elections, stressing that even a handful of illegal votes can decide tight races and erode confidence in the electoral system.

Texas‑Mexico bridges were shut for hours when Gulf Cartel gunmen terrorized Matamoros in an attempt to free the cartel boss’s son, highlighting cross‑border cartel threats and the need for strong security measures.
us_0036: Candy’s getting pricey – chocolate is up almost 8% this year because cocoa crops in West Africa got hit by drought and rain, pushing overall Halloween candy costs higher than regular food inflation, and the average spend is now about $115 per person.

The mass shooting at the Spirit Halloween in Fairfield was brutal; a customer said they thought the gunshots were balloons at first, then realized it was real, and the store stayed closed afterward out of respect for the victims.
Even with candy costs climbing, the National Retail Federation still predicts Americans will drop $13.5 billion on Halloween, a 3% rise, so folks aren’t ditching the holiday despite tighter wallets.

Israel’s election looks like it’ll end without a clear winner, with both right‑wing and left‑wing polls neck‑and‑neck, meaning there could be a drawn‑out coalition hunt while the country’s still fighting multiple wars.
us_0037: The U.N. report that Russia purposely bombed Ukraine’s power grid, leaving millions without heat in freezing weather, stuck with me; it shows how targeting energy can turn a winter into a humanitarian crisis.

The “stress‑free” paperwork guide’s advice to split documents into an “active” pile needing follow‑up and an “inactive” pile for filing reminded me of a simple way to keep track of things like my Social Security card.

Hearing that the Senate is unlikely to make daylight‑saving time permanent reminded me how changing the clocks twice a year still messes with early‑rising folks like me, especially when winter mornings stay dark.

The recent poll that 51 % of shoppers have stopped buying from companies because of their political stance made me think about how many people are now using their wallets to make a political point, even if intentions don’t always match actions.
us_0038: The FTC is suing Dollar General for systematically mislabeling shelf prices, which allegedly stole millions from shoppers who rely on low‑cost deals to stretch their paychecks.

Thirteen states will vote on local measures about data‑center construction, some forcing voter approval before a facility can be built, and the outcome could shape electricity rates and jobs in places like Ohio.
A recent poll found one‑in‑seven Americans trust AI chatbots as much as doctors, and most of those users say they’d follow the bot’s health advice even if it contradicts a medical professional.
Researchers showed two carrion crows beating humans at a rapid‑choice test, proving the birds can decide faster and more accurately than people, which is surprising for a non‑mammal brain.
us_0039: Trump tried to make the Iran war look “small” by comparing its 18 U.S. deaths to the thousands killed in Vietnam, saying the conflict would end soon, even though there’s no clear plan for how to pull out.

us_0123: The Justice Department’s rush to file high‑profile cases right before the midterms feels like a political play, especially the new probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar, which reminded me how federal actions can be timed for elections.

us_0149: The mortgage news that the 30‑year rate slipped to 7.24% for the first time in a month feels like a tiny break in the endless cost‑of‑living climb; even a half‑point drop makes a future home seem a little less impossible.
